Hey Coaches, our next presenter is Martin Roca. Martin is a world leader and innovator in the space of blue to green stage development within our sport, presenting at a multitude of conferences in Europe and Asia. Today Martin joins us to share some of his insights into the pathway to Yellow Ball. Welcome Martin. Hello friends, I'm Martin Roca, welcome to my presentation. I want to thank tennis Australia for the invitation once again to this conference. I'm thrilled and honored to be part of this lineup surrounded by amazing professionals. What I want to show you is the way I work with little kids. I've been coaching for 32 years now, I'm from Buenos Aires, Argentina. I worked there for eight years and then I moved to New York for five years. Now I live in Spain in the Barcelona area and I've been here for almost two decades. So grabbing ideas from different countries, different methodologies, that led to make me see the way I have to coach kids with a personal perspective. I call that mini players, it's like, you can call it philosophy or methodology, a system. I think it's the way I understand how we have to teach the kids in order to engage them in love this sport and practice it no matter what they are, if they're very skillful, if they're not, they have to learn how to play the sport and we have to get the best performance out of them. I see myself as a very technical coach.

I want my kids to have proper technique, proper footwork, good positioning on the court, a good understanding of the game, some things we don't teach that much and make them understand why they have to hit a cross court shot instead of a down the line according to the situation on the court, when they have to attack, when do they have to retrieve. We have to make them understand that they have to make decisions and we have to set up the training sessions for that. I want my kids also to have good behavior on the court, be respectful to everything related to the sport, coaches, teammates, opponents, umpires, facilities, equipment, they have to respect all of that, I'm very focused on that too. But I'm saying this because I see that we make the introduction to the sport very technical. I see the idea of, okay, I give you the tools so you can play better of the sport, so I'll give you, I'll teach you the technique first. What happens is, and it is my opinion, we make it too boring. We make it too technical in the beginning, so a three, four, five-year-old kid is coming with the idea of, okay, I'm going to play tennis and what they do is, you know, to stay on the line, they have one coach telling them, okay, point this hand towards the net, which in my opinion is a mistake. Get back, when I bounce the ball, you hit and follow through, okay, I understand, that's the idea. If you have the technique, you can play the sport better, but this is the introduction

You see kids coming with the idea of playing the sport and all of a sudden they find themselves standing still like a robot hitting or trying to hit a ball because sometimes they don't even hit it because it's the first time they grab a racket and they see a ball bouncing in front of them and they have to make contact and also they have to finish the shot because the coaches focus too much on the follow through. This is another topic we can discuss, but it's too mechanic in my opinion. We make it too boring, so in order to engage the kids, we have to do something different. We have to tell them, okay, we're going to let you play. We're going to give you some ideas. We're going to guide you, okay, this is the way you're going to hold the racket, this is the way you're going to toss the ball, this is the way you're going to play with your teammates, but we have to make it fun and also work on the electricity, work on the skills, work on their coordination because kids nowadays don't have the skills that kids have 30 years ago. Kids don't go out on the streets anymore. They don't play, they don't climb up trees. They don't play by themselves because parents go too fanatic about safety and safety measures and if they ride a bike, they have to wear a helmet and pass all over the body because they don't want them to get hurt. What we have to do in the sessions is to work on the coordination, work on the way they

move their body. They understand how to use their body, how to use an implement like a tennis racket on a tennis ball. And according to that, we are going to make them understand, enjoy the game and have fun but also improve their skills. What you see in this video is that you see kids three, four, five-year-olds in the same group doing the same tracks. Obviously, the goals that they have for each other, they're different, you have to adapt to their possibilities. Some of them will make it faster, some of them will take more time to do it, but you have to ask them to do what they can, not more than that. You obviously have to challenge them sometimes, but the thing is to maintain them doing activities all the time, always active, always in motion and reproducing mechanics that they wouldn't do when they play tennis. Also if you play games with them, try to engage them in team competitions because if you challenge them and they reach the goal, they consider as a team victory. This way, every play will feel important. As you can see in my sessions, every ball counts. So you don't see loose balls on the ground, every time they push the ball or they hit the ball, there's someone waiting for the ball to be hit. It's either a coach, it's either a teammate, sometimes they try to hit a cone, but every ball counts, it's important for them to understand that they cannot hit the ball hard and out

If we are talking about at this point, three, four, five, six-year-old kids that are playing Red Bull stage, what happens is they're playing a very small area. So if you don't prepare them to hit a ball in a small area under control, they're not going to be able to rally and don't forget that tennis is a game of interacting. You hit the ball and you wait for the ball to come back. So if you teach the kids to just hit the ball and pick up and go back to the line and hit 10 balls again, you're not preparing the kids to a proper game of tennis. They're just making contact or they're reproducing a shot or a mechanic, but they're not ready to interact, so you have to prepare them for that. As I was mentioning before, every time they hit the ball, the ball has a target and then that ball is being reused. Everything they do also is we work as a team and then if they do games, if they move around like in this one, the team has to accomplish a goal and every time they do it, you do it as a team. So that mentality helps them to understand that they don't have to be selfish. They have to work with their teammates and then cooperate, like when they pick up balls, when they collect the equipment or when they fix the core, there's always cooperation.

Something to discuss, coaches insisting too much on kids following through when they hit. For example, this three-year-old kid is hitting the ball in the target with only making contact, no backswing, no follow through. It's not necessary for him to go for a full swing because being a close range and hitting the ball in front, he can accomplish his goal of hitting the eye of the monster, as you can see right there. This is another case of a player who's not preparing the racket and not following through, but in my opinion she's playing tennis. I give her good feedback, so she's happy for what she's doing. She accomplishes the goal, she has to hit the ball back at me and the ball is under control. If you hit the ball 10 times and you're not worried about where the ball is landing and you have to pick up those balls and get back to the line, do you consider that that is playing tennis? In my opinion, this is playing tennis, exchanging shots with a teammate or with a coach and having fun with it. As we see these kids, there are different ages working on different skills, we're going to prepare for the orange ball group and the activities that we do with the kids. Orange ball kids, these kids have been playing with us for some years now, a couple of years probably, and they have basic skills of knowing how to use the implements, how to control the body, how to control the balance and how to hit the ball under control.

Now we have to teach in the basics the fundamentals, like for example in this case, split step, chasing a ball, ball tracking, hitting without losing balance, controlling the ball and recovery steps. Progressions allow coaches and players to reach their goals by simply following some steps. Coaches can increase the level of difficulties as the kids are doing fine the previous steps and for kids it's much better when they do everything little by little and so they can understand much better what they do and feel more confident about it. Now we're going to see a series of videos of this same girl, she's a seven year old player, as you can see we work a lot on fundamentals, split steps, good swing, feet moving all the time, good rhythm when she hits, ball control, she always hits the ball to me. Now we see this video was taken a few months later and then you see much more fluid swing, very intense when she hits, good ball control, personally I don't like feeding balls and not paying attention where the ball is landing. Now in this case we were working on the non-dominant hand, left hand in her case, trying to get more acceleration on the swing. She was using a lighter racket, a smaller one and then switching to her racket to get more power and fluid swing, get more speed on the left hand and this way I try to make it easier to understand how to get a more natural swing and get more speed with less

effort. Obviously we try to transfer that into a playing situation and for example if she needs to change directions she can go for a winner, like in this case. This is the case of many drills we do trying to think outside the box, trying to get them to be prepared for any situation and open the perspective, not always waiting for the ball, coming from the other side, using continental grip to get the wrist ready for any situation. In this particular progression we were working on the smash, in a fun way we were trying to get her under the ball using the head now, after that using the cone, just to catch the ball and get the body ready for contact, just focusing on the contact now, not following through, not reducing the full swing and then eventually trying to combine the volley and the smash in the proper positioning. One small advice for coaches, if you do this progression try to use sponge balls, so if you get hit you don't get hurt. As we move into the green ball group, you see we work on continental grip, this is part of the warm up they do every time they start a session, I do simple progressions with them even when they are in the red ball stage, to get amused to this grip, so that makes easier for them to handle the racket when they hit, for example, ball is in overhead, serves and also slides back ends. I really hope you enjoyed this presentation as much as I did, I'm a person that loves tennis and I like discussing with people about tennis and development ages or this presentation if you have questions, you want to debate, you want to exchange information, I'm always hoping to talk about that.
